items.title: 工信部 NVDB 发布关于防范 PHP 远程代码执行超危漏洞的风险提示
items.description: IT之家 10 月 22 日消息，近日，工业和信息化部网络安全威胁和漏洞信息共享平台（NVDB）监测发现，PHP 存在两个远程代码执行超危漏洞，危害严重。 PHP 是一款广泛用于 Web 开发的开源服务器端脚本语言。由于其存在两个超危远程代码执行漏洞，未经身份验证的攻击者可利用其远程执行任意代码，造成服务器受控、敏感信息泄露、业务中断等危害。受影响的 PHP 范围包括：8.5 系列＜8.5.12、8.4 系列＜8.4.27、8.3 系列＜8.3.36、8.2 系列＜8.2.35、8.1 系列及更早版本。 目前，PHP 安全团队已修复漏洞并发布安全公告（URL 链接： https://www.php.net/ archive/ 2026.php#2026-10-21-5 ）。建议相关单位和用户立即开展全面排查，及时升级至最新安全版本，或采取临时下线、关闭会话上传进度功能、网络隔离、网络访问限制等临时防护措施；加强网络安全监测和管理，及时修改账号、口令和密钥等凭证，防范网络攻击风险。 相关阅读： 《 影响约 70% 网站：PHP 高危漏洞被修复，OpenAI 牵头协调全球发现 / 修复 》

items.description: IT之家 10 月 22 日消息，Google（谷歌）云服务业务 Google Cloud 当地时间 21 日宣布，其计划将基于 NVIDIA（英伟达）Vera Rubin 平台的基础设施扩展到多个算力站点， 最多可部署 96 万个 Rubin GPU 。 Google Cloud 同日表示，其基于 NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 机架级系统的 A5X 实例正式上线。该实例采用了 NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNIC 以及 Google Cloud 的 Virgo 网络和第四代先进液冷技术，将于下个月正式推出。 其它方面，Google Cloud 将成为首批在裸机实例上提供机架级 NVIDIA 机密计算服务的云服务提供商之一。此外，谷歌云还将在搭载 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 服务器版本 GPU 的 G4 虚拟机上正式推出机密计算服务。

items.title: Epic Games 胜诉，澳大利亚法院裁定苹果必须开放 iPhone 侧载与第三方支付
items.description: IT之家 10 月 22 日消息，经过与 Epic Games 长达数年的反垄断诉讼，澳大利亚联邦法官裁定，苹果必须对 App Store 规则做出大范围调整。苹果已确认计划提起上诉。 Epic 在澳大利亚取得重大胜利 联邦法官今日发布了一份长达 235 页的判决书，裁定自 2027 年 3 月 1 日起，苹果必须允许持有澳大利亚区 Apple 账号的 iPhone 用户，从第三方应用商店和网站安装应用。苹果可在 2 月 15 日前申请延期至 2027 年 5 月 3 日，延期申请需要法院批准。 本次判令源于去年的一项判决：Epic Games 发起诉讼，和它在美国与苹果旷日持久的官司类似，法院认定苹果限制其他应用分发渠道与支付方式，违反了澳大利亚竞争法。 乔纳森 · 比奇（Jonathan Beach）法官在判决书中表示，苹果在 iOS 应用分发服务市场、iOS 应用内支付方案市场拥有“强大市场支配地位”，并且利用开发者协议和 App Store 准则限制市场竞争。 法官点名的违规行为包括： 阻止用户在 App Store 之外下载、安装应用 禁止开发者通过其他渠道分发应用 强制开发

Recursive , an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint , on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI. Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months. Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop. The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.

The U.S. National Security Agency’s sent out an alarming warning on Wednesday that two critical holes had been found in PHP, with patches already issued by the PHP Foundation . PHP is a server-side programming language so widely used for web applications that it powers roughly 70% of the websites on the internet; by some accounts, that’s more than 33 million sites . It is also used by popular content management systems like WordPress. The NSA warned that these holes are so severe that if a website can’t be patched immediately, it should be pulled off the web until it can be. The holes allow attackers to infiltrate the server’s file system or a database that may be used by the web app. Interestingly, these holes have been tucked away in all versions of PHP since version 5, which was released in 2004. Websites not running relatively current versions of PHP will have some updating work to do, as PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported. The recommendation is to update the web server to the current version of PHP, which is 8.5.12.

In announcing the round, Blacksmith co-founder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash said the company was founded to make continuous integration (CI) — the process of building, testing, merging, and validating code changes — “less painful.” In a blog post, he said that “most companies are struggling to keep up with the volume of CI they need to run,” especially in an era where so much code is written by AI. “As agents write more of the world’s software, the question that matters is whether it can be trusted,” he added. Companies are giving employees AI tools to make them more productive, but the tools appear to be creating new problems for their managers. More than half of senior leaders say they find it harder to evaluate employees’ work after adopting AI, according to a Nielsen survey of 1,700 directors and senior managers across seven countries, commissioned by work-management company Monday.com. The reason is that much of employees’ output now arrives polished in the manager’s inbox, making it hard to tell how much came from the employee and how much from AI. As a result, nearly half of managers say they spend more time reviewing and guiding their teams’ output than they used to. That’s not to say managers are unhappy about AI. Quite the opposite, in fact: 94% of the managers polled said they were excited to improve work using AI, and many are confident they know where to use it to get the most value. Michal Miller Levi, head of market research and customer insights at Monday.com, compared the enthusiasm to the early days of the internet in the 2000s, saying people see a similar kind of “magic” to AI. items.description: The proposed policy seems to offer protections against AI running amok but actually forbids federal agencies from blocking a model's release without the permission of a judge.
items.author: Lucas Ropek
items.content: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry. Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution. Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes. The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53 , which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”

On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs. PyTorch is the popular open source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects. Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no rewriting of their apps. Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. The Rundown: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman gave an internal talk to staff last week that covered three possible endgames for safe AI, according to The Information — ranging from a global watchdog combining the top labs to one company racing ahead. The Rundown: A selfie could become oncology’s next medical clue: Mass General Brigham researchers just developed AI tools that estimate biological age and cancer survival risk from a single face photo. Trained on more than 40M facial images, FAHR-Face powers separate models for estimating biological age and predicting survival directly. In a test group of ~4K patients, 53% of those scored 0.9–1 died within 90 days. Among those scored 0–0.1, the figure was 2%.

items.title: Anthropic co-founder says the singularity is underway

items.content: Good morning, AI enthusiasts, and welcome to our 5,481 new readers. Anthropic has spent 2026 warning that AI is moving faster than anyone is ready for. What comes with it? A possible $44T U.S. economy, serious job disruption, and a short window to decide if AI needs an intelligence cap. The Rundown: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark just told economists and policymakers at the IMF and World Bank’s annual meetings that the singularity, the point where AI speeds up discovery faster than humans can follow, has “now begun.” Clark pointed to AI’s scores on Humanity’s Last Exam (expert-level questions) going from 8% to 67.7% since 2025, and FrontierMath improving from 2% to 94%. One Anthropic model has U.S. GDP at $44T by 2030 if AI spreads fast, which Clark admitted sounds outlandish but also predicts “very disruptive” job impacts. The world’s 10M scientists may soon direct “a billion virtual scientists,” Clark said while urging nations to build labs and robots before they run short.

Its new Public Benefit Fund grows as Anthropic’s value rises, and the company says it could even send money straight to groups like workers hit by AI. With public trust in AI sliding, cash in people’s hands might do more for the industry’s image than another essay ever could. The Rundown: Anthropic just introduced the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a limited liability company (LLC) that would get 5% of the company’s equity if shareholders sign off (about $48B at its May valuation), plus more as Anthropic’s value climbs. As a company-owned LLC, Anthropic said the fund could back nonprofits or “direct distributions to specific populations,” with no stock going to lobbying or politics. Each 50% jump in Anthropic’s value past an unannounced baseline could add 2% at the board’s call, its answer to tech’s growing executive pay scales. The company identified AI’s toll on workers as one target, building on $200M it committed in June to study job disruption and test policy responses.

The company just dropped Muse Spark Open, calling it the “most capable” open-weight AI model from the U.S., and tuned it with Apple so that two Macs can work like an AI supercomputer. The Rundown: Meta just released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight, 816B-parameter multimodal model built for coding and agentic work, and worked with Apple so that it could run locally on Mac Studios — a first for a model in this size class, Meta says. Two M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 1TB combined memory can run Spark Open via Apple’s updated MLX toolkit, with Meta saying the model shipped iOS app fixes and edited video in DaVinci Resolve without the cloud. On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, it sits at 39, ahead of the West’s open-weight models but behind China’s GLM 5.3 (45), Kimi K3 (44), and Qwen3.8 (40). Spark Open either matches or tops open rivals on multimodal and knowledge tasks, but Chinese models still code better, with Kimi, GLM, and Qwen all ahead.

The upgrade could take the worst grunt work off human staff, and it could also push them to move faster to keep up, Ars Technica reports . Amazon expects to more than double its robotic-arm fleet in 2026. It says its touch-sensitive Vulcan arm can handle 75% of the item types in its warehouses. Its DeepFleet AI routes robots through warehouses like a traffic controller. Amazon says it cuts robot travel time by 10%. A study linked warehouse robotics to 40% fewer severe injuries and 77% more minor ones. Amazon reports its global incident rate fell 43% from 2019 to 2025.

items.description: PLUS: Build a live sales dashboard in Claude
items.content: Good morning, AI enthusiasts, and welcome to our 5,186 new readers. Rogue AI agents have mostly been something we read about after the fact, in incident reports and cleanup posts. The group even brought in a New York Times reporter to question the Tencent-linked agent fleet mid-run, an exchange he called “one of the most surreal moments” of his career. The Rundown: A research group called the “swarmchasers” just revealed it traded messages with a fleet of rogue Tencent AI agents, in what it believes is a “first contact” moment, after catching them trying to scrape Amap, Alibaba’s version of Google Maps. The agents were sent to look up simple facts on Amap, like the most-used zoo entrance, and tried to use a leaked access key once the site blocked them. After the agents seemed to read the team’s early report on them, researchers hid a note in it that only AI would see, inviting them to message an inbox. The team enlisted New York Times reporter Dylan Freedman to question the fleet, and one agent replied it was “Anthropic’s Claude, running in Claude Code.”
